Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:1: Having explained holiness, it is fitting to explain what pertains from it to practice. We shall say that the matter of the holiness concerning which we were commanded, "You shall be holy," is that a person separate himself from things that are mundane (chol), and sanctify his soul and body, for the opposite of chol is kodesh (holy) — as in the distinction of the Sabbath, which is called "holy" relative to the weekdays. And once we know what the holiness of the Sabbath is, we will know what this matter of holiness explained above is.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:2: Now, concerning the holiness of the Sabbath, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Emor 94a) in the distinction between "holy" and "holy convocations," explaining that the Sabbath is the very essence of the revealed holiness. Of this it is said, "And you shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you" (Exodus 31:14). And it says that the mystery of the Sabbath is the mystery of the son who ascends to his father's house without permission — this is "Who is like unto You, O Lord, among the mighty? Who is like unto You, majestic in holiness" (Exodus 15:11) — and it says "in holiness," definitely, for he has already grown strong in his father, "majestic in holiness," and does not need to be sanctified [again]. Then it says further: Rabbi Yehudah [said], the joy and the guarding of the day of Shabbat encompasses everything, because this day is crowned with Abba and Imma, and holiness is added upon its holiness, which is not found so on the other days; for it is holy, crowned with holiness, adding holiness upon its holiness. Because of this, this day is the joy of those above and those below — all rejoice in it, it is filled with blessings in all the worlds, all of them are established from it — so far his words. It is thus made clear that the holiness of the Sabbath is the light of the holiness of Abba and Imma, revealed in Tiferet and from there to all the worlds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:3: Further, concerning the holiness of the Sabbath and the other days, it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 204a) concerning the reality of the Sabbath: it is said that Malchut is the middle point of all six days, from which they nurse; and on the day of Shabbat she is the "pupil of the eye" (bat ayin), united with the three Patriarchs, who are called "Shin" — hence "Shabbat" is [an acrostic of] Shin-Bat. And there is a still higher "Shabbat" — three Patriarchs bound to the "pupil of the eye," bound to the World to Come. And there is a yet higher Shabbat, when all the aforementioned is bound to the supernal point, which is likewise the mystery of the "pupil of the eye." This is the abbreviated intent. It follows that wherever the son ascends, the daughter ascends there together with him above — so that always the mystery of the holiness of the Sabbath is the light flowing from Abba and Imma, and even higher, from Atika [Kadisha], who is the root of all holinesses and is called "the Holy Ancient One of Ancients," as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:4: And likewise it is further explained in Parashat Vayakhel (Zohar 205a), where they speak of the mystery of the conjugal duty (onah) of Torah scholars from Sabbath eve to Sabbath. And they say, what is the reason? Because on all the [other] days of the week there is a different spirit that rests upon the world, but on this night there is a different, holy, supernal spirit that descends to the holy children; and that spirit blows from the Holy Ancient One of all ancient ones and descends to the lower point, to give rest to all; and this spreads out in all directions, above and below, as it is said, "between Me and the children of Israel" — so far his words. And further on there it says: the day of Shabbat is joy for all, and all are lifted up, above and below, and the lower point shines to ascend above in the beauty of the seventy crowns, an extra portion, and the Ancient of all Ancients is aroused — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:5: Now, since the Sabbath is the root of all holinesses, we may say that the Torah's command "You shall be holy, for I am holy" means that we should sanctify ourselves and draw upon ourselves, each and every day, from the light of the holiness of the Sabbath — if we sanctify ourselves from doing labor, from purifying our thoughts, and from the other particulars that will be explained regarding the holiness of the Sabbath.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:6: There is an allusion to this in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro 89a), in these words: Rabbi Yehudah said, indeed it is written, "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Exodus 20:8), and it is written, "You shall be holy, for I the Lord am holy" (Leviticus 19:2), and it is written, "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight, holy of the Lord, honored" (Isaiah 58:13). We have learned: on this day, all the souls of the righteous delight in the delicacies of the Holy Ancient One, the concealed one of all concealed ones, and this spirit of delight spreads out into all the worlds, ascending and descending and spreading to all the holy children, to all who keep the Torah, and they rest in complete rest, and all anger, all judgments, and all harsh decrees are forgotten from all of them. This is what is written, "On the day the Lord gives you rest from your sorrow..." (Isaiah 14:3) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:7: His intent at the beginning of his words, where he says "indeed it is written, 'Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it,'" is that on the Sabbath day we were clearly warned to sanctify it, and its holiness is through our own self-sanctification. And so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Mechilta (Parashat Ki Tisa) on the verse, "And the children of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, to observe (la'asot) the Sabbath" (Exodus 31:16): Rabbi Elazar ben Parta said, whoever keeps the Sabbath is as if he made (created) the Sabbath, as it says, "to make the Sabbath" — so far his words. And his intent follows the pattern of what is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bechukotai 113a) on "and you shall do them" (Leviticus 26:3): it asks, what is the meaning of "and you shall do them"? Rather, whoever performs the precepts of the Torah and walks in its ways, it is as though he had, so to speak, made Him above; the Holy One, blessed be He, says, "It is as if he had made Me" — and so they established it. Hence "and you shall do them" — you shall indeed "do them," since you are aroused to join one thing with another, to glorify the holy Name as is fitting — "and you shall do them" indeed — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:8: Let us return to the matter: in saying "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it," its holiness is certainly explicit; but regarding the other days we have no proof that we need to sanctify them. From the verse's unqualified statement, "You shall be holy," the intent is regarding the holiness of all the days, and it brings [the phrase] "holy of the Lord, honored" to teach a verbal analogy (gezerah shavah) from "for I am holy" — for just as the verse "holy of the Lord, honored" refers to the day of Shabbat, based on the preceding "And you shall call the Sabbath a delight," so the verse "for I am holy" means that everything is holy with the holiness of Shabbat, for Shabbat is the root of all holinesses. Therefore it brings the proof: "We have learned, on this day the souls of the righteous delight in the delicacies of the Holy Ancient One, the concealed one of all concealed ones," and it says that on Shabbat this light spreads through all the worlds; therefore the day of Shabbat is holy of itself, its holiness not being in the hands of the court [to fix], unlike the sanctification of the festivals, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in the Mechilta (Parashat Ki Tisa). And this is what the verse means by "for I am holy" — in the manner explained, of blessed memory, in the passage we quoted in the preceding chapter, which said: or is it perhaps that if you sanctify Me, I am indeed sanctified, and if not, I am not sanctified? The verse teaches, "for I am holy" — in My holiness I stand, whether they sanctify [Me] or whether they do not sanctify [Me]. We thus learn from the whole of his words that a person is obligated to sanctify the six weekdays from the holiness of the Sabbath day.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:9: This is likewise explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel 204a), in these words: Come and see, the supernal mystery of the matter: all these six days, the matter stands that everything is united in the mystery of one holy point, and all the days are united in it. And there are other days that stand outside on the other side, and there are six other days that stand within the holy circle and are united with the holy point. And Israel, who are holy, and all those who occupy themselves with holiness all the days of the week, unite all those six days with those six inner days, which are united with that point; they unite with this in order to be guarded by it. And all through those six days that point is hidden; once Shabbat enters, then that point rises and is crowned and unites above, and all are hidden within it. Come and see, there are [ordinary] days and there are [other] days: the weekdays are as stated, and these stand outside forever; the days of Shabbat — which are the days of the week — belong to Israel; and when this point rises, everything is concealed, and it ascends — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:10: His intent is that there are three kinds of days: the first, the weekdays that stand outside holiness, belonging to the idolatrous nations — meaning that to the idolatrous nations were given the thirty-nine labors, which correspond to the thirty-nine curses with which Adam, Eve, the serpent, and the earth were cursed, as is explained, of blessed memory (Tikkunei Zohar 85a). Had Adam not sinned, he would not have needed to descend to this lowly state in which he must plow and sow; he would have been in the Garden of Eden, fulfilling "to work it and to guard it" through the performance of the positive and negative commandments in a spiritual manner, as will be in the future after the resurrection — for the Torah and its commandments are one, forever. But when Adam descended through his sin to the kelipah, he was forced into these labors.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:11: And the Holy One, blessed be He, in order to purify and sanctify us so that we might be able to cleave [to Him], raised us up above the six outer days and gave Israel a governance of holiness through Metatron, who is the Prince of the World, as it was said to Joshua, "I am the captain of the host of the Lord; now I have come" (Joshua 5:14) — for even though Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, pushed him away, he was forced to accept him; and all the more so now, in exile, when the governance is through him, as is explained in the Tikkunim (14b) and in other places (Ra'aya Meheimna, Parashat Pinchas 215a). And on the six weekdays the governance is through Metatron, as is likewise explained in Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas 243b), and also in the Tikkunim (2b), in these words: the bird, whose bird it is, is Metatron; of him it is said, "For a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice" (Ecclesiastes 10:20) — the voice of the recitation of the Shema, which encompasses the six weekdays and rules over them, and takes that voice and flies with it until the middle pillar — so far his words. And further on it says that through this messenger unification is achieved on the six weekdays. And the phrase "six weekdays" is not exactly parallel to what we said in the passage from Parashat Vayakhel, that the weekdays are called "outer"; rather the intent is that on the six weekdays the world is governed by the aforementioned prince, and through him our prayer ascends.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:12: And so it says in the manuscript Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 106b), that concerning him it is said, "Six days shall you labor and do all your work" (Exodus 20:9), in these words: On the weekdays the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil ascends, which is Adam, "and He formed [vayyitzer]" with the good inclination and the evil inclination — this is what is written, "And the Lord God formed [vayyitzer] man" (Genesis 2:7) — and it is the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil through which Adam sinned. This is Metatron, who is a servant who rules over the six orders of the Mishnah, and is corporeal, and rules over the six weekdays, which are mundane matters of impurity and mundane matters of purity; and from him were given the six orders of the Mishnah, dealing with forbidden and permitted, impure and pure, fit and unfit; and through him [it is fulfilled], "Six days shall you labor and do all your work." And there is no [true] service except prayer, in which a person must be like a servant arranging his praises before his master, and like a servant asking for a stipend from his master, and like a servant who receives a stipend from his master and goes his way. But on Shabbat, Malkat (the Queen) rules, the Tree of Life, and not the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil — and they established that one must not make any use of the Tree — so far his words. It is thus made clear that the whole reality of the service of prayer is through this servant on the six weekdays; but on Shabbat, the light of Atzilut (Emanation) rules. By this we can understand the phrase, "And the seventh day is a Sabbath unto the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:10) — that the whole intent of the prayer is to be in Atzilut, and Atzilut is clothed in Beriah (Creation), which is "the Lord your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:13: Incidentally, it is made clear that this servant is called "the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil," and it is said in the Tikkun (Tikkunei Zohar 87b): "Tree of Knowledge" — "good" is Metatron, and "evil" is Samael. And the sin of Adam was to mix the evil with the good; therefore, in this place there are the six orders of the Mishnah, to separate the good by itself and the evil by itself. And so it further says there (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash): the tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil needs to have a separation made between good and evil — this is what is written, "And God separated between the light and the darkness" (Genesis 1:4) — and one must make an excision within it, that a person be without the evil inclination, in the manner of David, who cut it off from himself and killed it through his study — this is what is written, "And my heart is empty (a corpse) within me" (Psalms 109:22); and corresponding to the forty-nine [aspects] of Metatron are the forty-nine faces of pure and forty-nine faces of impure — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:14: Incidentally, it is made clear that the special property of studying the Mishnayot is to kill and subdue the evil inclination; even though these Mishnayot, containing the disputes of the Tannaim, did not yet exist in David's time, nevertheless he had six orders of fixed halachot (rulings), and he studied them — so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:15: Now, given what is explained in this passage — that Metatron is called "good and evil," and it is said also that he rules over the weekdays, and that there are mundane matters of impurity and mundane matters of purity — in the same manner, in the passage from Parashat Vayakhel, there are weekdays among the outer [forces], and there are inner ones, the six days of the week that are in purity, for the governance of Israel; and these two aspects are like the tree and its bark — good on the inside and evil on the outside — the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:16: And it says that these six days are held fast to the holy point; it appears from the wording that this point is the Shechinah, who is concealed within Metatron, within the palace of the "bird's nest," as is explained in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 102a), and Metatron consists of six chambers corresponding to the six weekdays, and in the seventh chamber the Shechinah is concealed there; and on the six weekdays the Shechinah is a point concealed within these six days, and the days shine from her, and she, in concealment, gives forth flow to each and every one of the days.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:17: And there are six days in Atzilut, which are the six extremities from Chesed to Yesod, which performed all the acts of creation, concerning which it is said, "For in six days the Lord made the heavens and the earth" (Exodus 31:17) — "in the six" is not said, as is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi 247a). Of these it says, "And there are six other days that stand within the holy circle and are united with the holy point." And it says "holy circle," for these are the six extremities that form the reality of the circle, which is holy, in the place of holiness in Atzilut; and the Shechinah is an inner point to them, from which they nurse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:18: Now, on the day of Shabbat, Malchut, who is below a concealed point, ascends above into Atzilut; and what had been a concealed point now spreads out in her light, and all the days become concealed within her, and she in her abundant light shelters over them. This is the meaning of "once Shabbat enters, then that point rises and is crowned and unites above, and all are hidden within it." And this is what is explained in the Tikkunim, which I quoted above: that on the weekdays the governance is through Metatron, and on the day of Shabbat the governance is through the light of Atzilut, which is the Tree of Life.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:19: And likewise it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Noach 75b), regarding the matter of "the gate of the inner court that faces east shall be shut the six working days, but on the Sabbath day..." (Ezekiel 46:1). And the abbreviated intent is that the gate of the inner court is the light of Atzilut, and it is shut on the six working days, which is the governance through Metatron; and on the Sabbath day it is opened, and the six working days have no rule at all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:20: And it says further on: and all the days cleave to the day of Shabbat and are nourished from there, for then, on the day of Shabbat, all the gates are opened, and rest is found for all, above and below. This passage is made clear by what was explained in the passage from Parashat Vayakhel, which we wrote — that on the day of Shabbat the six days become concealed within the point, and the point, which is the light of the Shechinah in Atzilut, shines upon them, and from her they nurse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:21: What pertains to our discourse is what is said in the passage from Parashat Vayakhel: "Israel, who are holy, and all those who occupy themselves with holiness all the days of Shabbat, unite all those six days with those six inner days that are united with that point." The intent is that they bind the six weekdays that are within Metatron, the six chambers, with the six sefirot of the Structure (Binyan) in Atzilut, so that the light of Atzilut may shine within them; and this is certainly through the intention of prayer, as is explained in Parashat Pekudei — that through the intention of the blessings of the Shema and the Amidah, the chambers are bound and made to shine with the light of Atzilut; and by this we separate the good from the evil, and the good is sanctified with the light of the good that is in Atzilut, and by this they are guarded from the evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:22: The reason is that the six days, even though they are in Atzilut, do not have the actual holiness of the Sabbath day — but rather, on the six weekdays, when the governance is below, even the six supernal extremities of Atzilut nurse from the point, and each and every day rules in its own dominion — Chesed on the first day, Gevurah on the second day, and so on — and the point is concealed within them; whereas on the day of Shabbat the point spreads out in its light, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:23: And the reason we need to bind the six lower days to the six upper ones is that on the six weekdays labor is permitted, because the governance is through the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. This is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, was precise about in the Tikkunim (Tikkunei Zohar Chadash 106b), where he says that Metatron rules over the six weekdays, which are the mundane matters of impurity and the mundane matters of purity — meaning precisely the six outer days, the mundane matters of impurity, which are the thirty-nine labors, and the mundane matters of purity, the six inner days from the "good" within Metatron; and the mundane matters of impurity and the mundane matters of purity, both together, rule — and therefore labor is permitted. And Israel were warned to sanctify themselves, as the verse says, "You shall be holy" — meaning, that they should sanctify the pure mundane [days] with the light of the holiness of Atzilut, which is entirely holy and has no contact with the mundane, and let the holiness of the six upper days shine into the six lower days, and by this they become sanctified. And the light of Shabbat, which is the gate facing east — even though it is shut the six working days, Israel draw from the light of the six sefirot of Atzilut to sanctify what is mundane. And they explained a similar point there (Zohar Parashat Noach 75b): that even though we say it is shut the six days, the intent is not that the light of Atzilut is entirely sealed off, which would suggest a withdrawal of [divine] providence, but rather that the supernal light is concealed within, and it is like the throne of the king who is within his palace and commands his servants to do such-and-such — so that whatever is done, all is done by the king's decree. My teacher, peace be upon him, further explained that this is comparable to a king who sometimes uses vessels of silver or vessels of copper, and sometimes vessels of gold; and the meaning of the parable is understood.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:24: And regarding the reality of the holiness of the six weekdays that was explained, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Mechilta (Parashat Yitro), in these words: "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" — you shall remember it from the first day of the week, so that if a fine portion should come your way, you should set it aside for the sake of Shabbat. Rabbi Yitzchak said, you should not count [the days] the way others count, but rather you should count for the sake of Shabbat — so far their words. The intent of the first opinion (tanna kamma) and Rabbi Yitzchak is one and the same matter — to explain what this remembrance is, and further, [to explain] the extra word "et" mentioned in the verse. And to this he said that the intent is to remember the holiness of Shabbat throughout all six days, so that if a fine portion comes your way, you should set it aside for Shabbat; and just as, in the physical sense, one sets aside and consecrates the fine portion for Shabbat, so should one prepare his soul that the holiness of Shabbat may rest upon it. And the reason is that Shabbat is analogous to the World to Come, and just as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, compared this world and the World to Come to Sabbath eve and Shabbat, saying (Avodah Zarah 3a), "Whoever toils on Sabbath eve shall eat on Shabbat, but whoever does not toil on Sabbath eve, what shall he eat on Shabbat?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:25: And so they also said in the Mechilta (Parashat Ki Tisa) on "for I the Lord sanctify you" (Exodus 31:13): our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, "For I the Lord sanctify you" for the World to Come, just as [I sanctify you with] the holiness of Shabbat in this world; we thus learn that it is a foretaste of the holiness of the World to Come. And so it says, "A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day" (Psalms 92:1) — for the world that is entirely Shabbat — so far their words. And the plain meaning of the passage that says "just as the holiness of Shabbat in this world" is to resolve the understanding of the verse, which says, "You shall surely keep My Sabbaths, for it is a sign between Me and you throughout your generations, to know that I the Lord sanctify you" (Exodus 31:13), and then it says, "And you shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you..." (v.14). Two things should be noted: first, how do we know that He sanctifies us because we keep the Sabbath? For with all the commandments He, blessed be He, sanctifies us, as we bless over all the commandments, "who has sanctified us with His commandments." And further, it seems superfluous, since it already says afterward, "And you shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you." Therefore it explains that the meaning of "for I the Lord sanctify you" is to give the reason for keeping the Sabbath, namely: "for I the Lord sanctify you" for the World to Come, just as [I sanctify you with] the holiness of Shabbat in this world — meaning, just as I have sanctified you with the holiness of Shabbat in this world, I am destined to sanctify you in the World to Come. And the holiness of Shabbat in this world is that through a person's keeping the Sabbath properly he will feel an added soul within himself — this is "and was refreshed [vayinafash]" (Exodus 31:17), which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Beitzah 16a), and it is a delight for the soul and the body, to the point that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 57b) that the Sabbath is one sixtieth of a foretaste of the World to Come — for the rest and delight that the righteous person feels in it is one sixtieth of that wondrous delight. And the reason is that in this world, because of its physicality, we cannot attain more than this, for the soul is clothed in this material body; but once the soul removes this turbid garment, it will attain the delight of the World to Come in its fullness. This is the meaning of "we thus learn that it is a foretaste of the holiness of the World to Come."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:26: By this we understand what the verse says afterward, "between Me and the children of Israel it is a sign forever" — the intent being that Shabbat is a sign and proof to us forever, of the world that is entirely long [i.e., eternal], for from this foretaste of rest will come the rest that is to come. And further, just as Shabbat comes after six days, so after six thousand years the world exists and one [thousand years] is desolate, which is comparable to Shabbat — for just as the six days rest on the Sabbath, so all the six thousand years rest in the one that is desolate; and just as during the six days one must prepare for Shabbat, whether regarding eating or regarding deeds, as will be further explained, so if one does not set his deeds right in this world, he will have nothing to eat in the World to Come. This is the meaning of "so I am destined to sanctify you in the World to Come."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:27: It follows that the verse is connected with what precedes it, "to know...," and "And you shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you" — and by keeping the day that is holy we know that He, blessed be He, will in the future sanctify us in the World to Come. This is the meaning of "we thus learn that it is a foretaste of the holiness of the World to Come."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:28: Now, since we know that Shabbat is a foretaste of the holiness of the World to Come, the divine intent in giving us the holiness of the Sabbath was to teach us that a person's main dwelling is not in this world — for in this world he is a sojourner, as we have elaborated above — and his essential place is in the world of souls, which is the World to Come. Therefore he rests from labor, which represents the affairs of the world, and he sanctifies the Sabbath day to show that he is being sanctified and has no dealings with the affairs of this world, for the whole reality of holiness is separation, as is known.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:29: And since this is the intent of the holiness of the Sabbath, every day one is obligated to think of and remember the holiness of the Sabbath, so that he will remember the matters of his end, in the manner of what they said (Shabbat 153a), "Repent one day before your death — repent today," and so on. This is the meaning of "you should remember it from the first day of the week, so that if a fine portion comes your way," and so on. And in this manner one should remember, from the first day of the week — meaning, in his youth — what he will in the future need to prepare as a fine portion for his soul, for the world that is entirely Shabbat and entirely long.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:30: And I heard from the honorable Rabbi Avraham HaLevi, may his light shine, that concerning this Shammai said (Beitzah 16a), "From the first day of your week [prepare] for your Sabbath" — for the six days [of life] are sixty years, which is the lifespan of most people, and "from the first day of your week," which is the first ten years, one must prepare provisions for his journey. Concerning this it is said, "Six days shall you labor and do all your work" (Exodus 20:9), and it says "all your work," with the extra word "lecha" ("your," for you) — meaning the spiritual labor, the labor of Torah and commandments, which is truly yours and not for another, unlike the other, physical labors, all of which remain for another. And so it says of the manna, "Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there shall be none" (Exodus 16:26) — alluding to the world that is entirely Shabbat, where there is no performing of Torah and commandments, only the receiving of reward, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained: "Whoever toils on Sabbath eve shall eat on Shabbat," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:31: And Rabbi Yitzchak said, that one should not count the way others count, but should count for the sake of Shabbat. He gave another, very easy remembrance for all the days — for if the remembrance depended on whether a fine portion comes his way, sometimes it comes and sometimes it does not. Therefore he said that one should count for the sake of Shabbat — counting on the first day, "today is the first day of the [week toward] Shabbat," "today is the second day toward Shabbat," "the third toward Shabbat," and so on — so that he mentions the name of Shabbat every single day.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:32: According to what was explained above, that all the days nurse from the day of Shabbat, and that the day of Shabbat is the central point around which the circle of the six days revolves — [diagram] — it follows that Shabbat is the root of the root of all six days of the week, and therefore every single day one is obligated to draw an influx from the holiness of Shabbat into it, as will be explained. For this reason Rashbi, peace be upon him, was precise in the wording of the passage I quoted above from Parashat Vayakhel, saying, "the days of Shabbat, which are the days of the week, belong to Israel" — behold, he called them "days of the week" and also "days of Shabbat." The reason, as explained, is that the point that is the Shabbat is concealed within the days of the week, and therefore they are called "days of Shabbat."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:33: And so I found that Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, wrote that the day of Shabbat is the central point of a circle, in these words: The whole of creation, and all the existing things that the Holy One, blessed be He, created — all of them are the mystery of a sphere (galgal); and He created everything at one point, which is the mystery of Shabbat, and it is the mystery of the reality of the "eye" of every sphere. And once Shabbat exists, which is the mystery of the point of every sphere, the six weekdays are found around it, and Shabbat, in the middle, is called "holy," having no counterpart; and it is the source of all the flow and all the goodness for the sphere. There is no sphere that does not contain the mystery of Shabbat, and the six weekdays all revolve around the circle in a fixed measure, upon which nothing may be added and from which nothing may be subtracted — for according to the measure of the middle point, so are the six measures of it around the circle, and all of them are called "the hollow of the circle" (chalal ha'igul), called "chalal" in the sense of "chillul" (desecration/hollowing), and "chillul" in the sense of "chalal" (a hollow/a corpse) — all one term; for once the middle eye is removed, all are found to be hollow, desecrated, and empty (chalalim) — for one is called a "corpse" (chalal) once his soul has already left him, and the body is found hollow, without the middle point. And this is the mystery of "six days shall be mundane, and the seventh day holy" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:34: Now, from the reason the Rabbi, of blessed memory, wrote, there is support and confirmation for what I have written — that one must draw an influx from the holiness of the day of Shabbat into every single day, since the point is what sustains the six, and the six are six measures around the point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:35: And I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him, that concerning this our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 69b): one who walks in the desert and does not know when the day of Shabbat is, should count seven days from the day he became aware of his forgetfulness, and sanctify the seventh — performing Kiddush and Havdalah. Here it is explicit that he is permitted to make a Shabbat even though in truth it is not [really] Shabbat; and the reason is that the middle point, which is Shabbat, accompanies all the days to give them influx, and every single day has within it a portion of Shabbat; therefore, on every single day, he should not do more labor than is necessary for his sustenance, because every day is a doubtful Shabbat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:36: As for the practical application, we may say: this world is comparable to the desert, and a person in it has been driven from his place of rest, the rest of the soul; and in this world, being drawn after the darkness by the counsel of his evil inclination, he has forgotten the day of Shabbat — the day that is entirely Shabbat, which is the world of souls where his true dwelling is. Therefore, from the day he becomes aware of his forgetfulness and wishes to return in repentance, he must always keep his garments clean, and every day he should think that it is Shabbat, lest that very day happen to be the [final] world that is entirely Shabbat, as they said, "Repent one day before your death." Therefore he should not do more labor than necessary for his sustenance for that day, as one who happens to be on a journey, for perhaps he has no life except that day alone, and it is not fitting that he should toil and worry over a world that is not his — as King David, peace be upon him, said, "and leave their wealth to others" (Psalms 49:11), and likewise, "he heaps up riches and does not know who will gather them" (Psalms 39:7). And they said (Gittin 47a) that Reish Lakish left behind a kav of turmeric — that is, zafaran (saffron) — and recited over it, "and leave their wealth to others."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:37: Further, they said in tractate Eruvin (54a), in these words: Shmuel said to Rav Yehudah, "Sharp one, snatch and eat, snatch and drink, for the world from which we depart is like a wedding feast." Rav said to Rav Hamnuna: "My son, if you have [means], do good for yourself, for there is no pleasure in the grave, and death does not delay. And if you say, 'I will leave [an inheritance] for my children' — who will tell you the law in the grave? And if you say, 'I will leave it for my sons and my daughters' — human beings are like the grasses of the field: these blossom and those wither" — so far his words. And Rashi explained: "snatch and eat" — if you have money to enjoy yourself, do not wait until tomorrow, lest you die and no longer have the enjoyment. "The world from which we depart" is the reading, "is like a wedding feast" — here today and gone tomorrow. "If you have" — money. "And death does not delay" — an interval, for a person dies suddenly. "The law" — sustenance; "who will tell you" — if it remains in their hands, perhaps they will lose it. "These blossom and those wither" — that is, as they grow, their livelihood and wealth grow with them, and you need not worry over them — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:38: One must "sanctify the seventh" — that one day of the week he should sanctify entirely to the Lord, corresponding to the many days he wasted in vain in the service of the foreign god within him; and we have already elaborated in the Gate of Awe (ch. 9) that he is punished in Gehinnom day for day, or two for one. Therefore he must sanctify one day to the service of his Maker, with the holiness of the Sabbath day, in the holiness of speech and of [refraining from] labor that interrupts a person's attachment to his Maker. Therefore it is good that he seclude himself in a special place and sanctify all his senses properly. The day of Shabbat alone will not suffice for a penitent, for the day of Shabbat was given to him as if he had not sinned; but after he has sinned and blemished so many days, he must sanctify at least one day a week to the Lord, and more if he is able.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:39: And so it says in the Zohar (beginning of Parashat Acharei Mot) that there were two merchants who withdrew from settled society two days a week to occupy themselves with Torah. In these words, concerning Rabbi Chiya, who was on the road and found two men in a rock valley, and said, "I approached them and said to them, 'What is your occupation in this place?'" They said, "We are merchants, and two days a week we separate ourselves from settled society and occupy ourselves with Torah, because people do not leave us alone every single day." I said, "Fortunate is your portion" — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 2:40: And holiness should be in moderation, so that any person can fulfill it and persevere in it — for if he wishes to separate himself all the days of the week, he will not persevere and will end up idle from everything. Therefore it is fitting to take hold of holiness little by little, and to learn from these men of deeds mentioned above — for what profit does a person have from all his toil that he toils under the sun, and he has nothing in his world except what he sanctifies and separates from the affairs of this world and attaches to the Name, blessed be He.
